config.title: Discriminated Union Props

intro.title: Discriminated Union Props
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a simple notification component that displays different types of messages (like success, warning, or error). You will learn how to use a TypeScript feature called a discriminated union to define the component's props, ensuring that each message type has its own specific properties. This involves creating a union type with a common 'kind' property that TypeScript can use to distinguish between the different shapes. By the end, you'll understand how to write type-safe React components that handle multiple, distinct prop structures cleanly and effectively.
intro.usecase: Discriminated union props are essential when building UI components that need to handle multiple distinct states or variants in a type-safe way. You'll see this pattern in dashboard components that display different card types (metrics, charts, tables), form systems with conditional fields that change based on user selections, and notification components that render success, warning, or error messages with different styling and behavior. This approach ensures TypeScript can validate that you're using the correct properties for each variant, preventing runtime errors when components switch between different modes or states.

objectives: Define a discriminated union type with a common discriminant property to represent different component states.
Apply TypeScript type annotations to declare component props that accept a discriminated union.
Implement conditional rendering logic using the discriminant property to display different UI elements.
Utilize type narrowing with switch statements to handle each variant of the discriminated union safely.
Construct component interfaces that include both shared properties and variant-specific properties.
Use exhaustive type checking patterns to ensure all union variants are handled in rendering logic.
Assign appropriate TypeScript generics to component definitions that accept discriminated union props.
Invoke components with different discriminated union variants and observe the resulting rendered output.
Control component behavior by modifying the discriminant property value passed as props.
Return JSX elements conditionally based on the active variant of the discriminated union.
Compare type safety benefits between discriminated unions and regular union types in component props.
Modify existing component props to use discriminated unions for improved type safety and developer experience.

steps.title: Import React from 'react'
steps.instruction: Import React from the 'react' package to enable JSX syntax and component creation.
steps.hint: Use the import statement to bring React into your file. This is required for any component that uses JSX.
steps.analogousExample:
// Import React to use JSX and create components
import React from 'react';
steps.expectedOutcome: The file will have React imported, allowing you to write JSX in the next steps.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully imported React. This is the foundation for writing JSX and creating components in TypeScript.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you're importing React specifically from the 'react' package using the correct syntax.
steps.feedbackWrong: That doesn't look right. Remember to import React from the 'react' package to use JSX in your TypeScript components.

steps.title: Create the main component
steps.instruction: Create a functional component named 'App' that returns null for now. Use TypeScript syntax.
steps.hint: Define a function or arrow function named App that returns null. Remember to import React if needed.
steps.seedCode:
import React from 'react';

// Create the App component here
steps.expectedOutcome: The App component is defined and returns null.
successCriteria: The code includes a functional component named App that returns null.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created the App component. Returning null for now is fine—we'll add content in later steps.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure the component is named exactly 'App' and returns null.
steps.feedbackWrong: The component isn't defined correctly. Check that you've created a function named App that returns null.

steps.title: Define a discriminated union type
steps.instruction: Define a TypeScript type named 'Message' that is a discriminated union of two object types. Both types should have a common 'type' property with literal string values ('success' and 'error'), and each should have additional properties specific to that variant.
steps.hint: Use the 'type' keyword to create a union type. Define two object types with a 'type' property that has a literal string value, then combine them with the '|' operator.
steps.expectedOutcome: You should have a 'Message' type that can be either a success message with a 'content' property or an error message with an 'errorCode' property, distinguished by the 'type' property.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Perfect! You've created a proper discriminated union type. The 'type' property acts as the discriminant that TypeScript can use to narrow down which variant you're working with.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check: Did you use the 'type' keyword? Is it a union of two object types? Do both have a 'type' property with literal string values? Do they have different additional properties?
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's try again. You need to define a TypeScript type named 'Message' that is a union of two object types. Both should have a 'type' property (with values like 'success' and 'error'), plus different additional properties for each variant.

steps.title: Create a component that accepts the union type as props
steps.instruction: Create a new functional component named 'MessageDisplay' that accepts a prop called 'message' of type 'Message' (the discriminated union type you defined earlier). The component should return a simple <div> element for now.
steps.hint: Define a component with typed props. You can use either a function declaration or arrow function syntax.
steps.expectedOutcome: A MessageDisplay component is defined with typed props matching the Message union type.
successCriteria: Component is a valid TypeScript function/arrow function
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created a component that accepts the discriminated union type as props. This is the foundation for type-safe component design with unions.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check: Did you name the component 'MessageDisplay'? Does it accept a 'message' prop of type 'Message'? Does it return JSX?
steps.feedbackWrong: The component isn't quite right. Make sure you create a component named 'MessageDisplay' that takes a prop called 'message' with type 'Message' and returns JSX.

steps.title: Add conditional rendering based on the discriminant
steps.instruction: In your MessageDisplay component, use the 'type' property from props to conditionally render different content. Start by checking if props.type equals 'success' and return a success message.
steps.hint: Use an if statement or switch statement to check props.type. For now, just handle the 'success' case by returning a JSX element like a green paragraph.
steps.expectedOutcome: The MessageDisplay component will now check the 'type' property and render different content for the 'success' case.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added conditional rendering based on the discriminant property. This allows TypeScript to narrow the type safely.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're checking props.type and returning JSX specifically for the 'success' case.
steps.feedbackWrong: Try using an if statement to check if props.type equals 'success', then return a paragraph element with a success message.

steps.title: Initialize state with a message
steps.instruction: In the App component, use the useState hook to create a state variable called 'message' that will store a value of the Message union type. Initialize it with an object that has type: 'success' and text: 'Operation completed!'.
steps.hint: You'll need to import useState from 'react' and call it with an initial value that matches the Message type.
steps.expectedOutcome: The App component will have a state variable 'message' initialized with a success message object.
successCriteria: The code should include: 1) useState import from 'react', 2) A state variable declaration for 'message' using useState, 3) The initial value should be an object with type: 'success' and text: 'Operation completed!'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully initialized state with a message object that matches the Message union type. This gives us data to pass to our MessageDisplay component.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but something is missing. Make sure you've: 1) Imported useState from 'react', 2) Declared a state variable called 'message' using useState, 3) Initialized it with an object that has type: 'success' and text: 'Operation completed!'.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's focus on this specific step. We need to initialize state with a message object. Start by importing useState from 'react', then declare a state variable called 'message' and initialize it with { type: 'success', text: 'Operation completed!' }.

steps.title: Create a handler to change the message type
steps.instruction: Inside your App component, create a function named handleChangeMessage that takes a parameter of type Message and calls setMessage with that parameter.
steps.hint: The function should accept a Message object and update the state using the setMessage function.
steps.expectedOutcome: You'll have a handler function that can update the message state with different discriminated union variants.
successCriteria: The handler function should be defined inside the App component, accept a Message parameter, and call setMessage with that parameter.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created a handler function that can update the message state with different discriminated union variants.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your handler function accepts a Message parameter and calls setMessage with it.
steps.feedbackWrong: The handler function should accept a Message parameter and update the state using setMessage. Try creating a function like: handleChangeMessage(newMessage: Message) { setMessage(newMessage); }

steps.title: Add the MessageDisplay component to App
steps.instruction: In the App component's return statement, render the MessageDisplay component and pass the message state as props.
steps.hint: Use JSX syntax to include the MessageDisplay component and pass the message state variable as props.
steps.expectedOutcome: The MessageDisplay component will be rendered inside App with the current message state passed as props.
successCriteria: The App component's return statement includes the MessageDisplay component with the message state passed as props.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully rendered the MessageDisplay component and passed the message state as props.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're rendering MessageDisplay inside App's return statement and passing the message state as props.
steps.feedbackWrong: The MessageDisplay component isn't properly rendered or the props aren't passed correctly. Check that you're using JSX syntax to include the component.

steps.title: Add a button to toggle to the first variant
steps.instruction: Inside the App component's return statement, add a button element with the text 'Show Success Message' and an onClick handler that calls changeMessageType with 'success' as the argument.
steps.hint: Add a button element inside the div. Use onClick={() => changeMessageType('success')} or create a separate inline function.
steps.expectedOutcome: The App component will have a button that, when clicked, changes the message state to a success variant.
successCriteria: The button element must be present with the text 'Show Success Message' and an onClick handler that calls changeMessageType('success').
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've added a button that triggers the state change to the success variant.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure your button has the correct text and onClick handler that calls changeMessageType('success').
steps.feedbackWrong: Check that you added a button element with the text 'Show Success Message' and an onClick handler that calls changeMessageType('success').

steps.title: Add a button to toggle to the second variant
steps.instruction: Add a second button in your App component's return statement that, when clicked, changes the message to the 'error' variant.
steps.hint: Add a <button> element with an onClick handler that calls changeMessageType with 'error' as the argument.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of adding a button for a different variant
<button onClick={() => changeMessageType('error')}>
  Show Error Message
</button>
steps.expectedOutcome: A second button appears in the UI that, when clicked, changes the message to an error variant.
successCriteria: Set its onClick handler to call changeMessageType('error')
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've added a button to toggle to the error variant. This gives users a way to switch between both discriminated union types.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure you have a button element with an onClick handler that calls changeMessageType('error').
steps.feedbackWrong: Try adding a button element with an onClick handler that calls changeMessageType('error').

steps.title: Add a wrapper div and structure
steps.instruction: Wrap the existing MessageDisplay component and the two buttons inside a <div> element with a class name of 'message-container'.
steps.hint: Add a <div> with className='message-container' around the MessageDisplay component and the two buttons.
steps.analogousExample:

Content
steps.expectedOutcome: The MessageDisplay component and both buttons are now wrapped inside a div with the class 'message-container'.
successCriteria: The code should contain a <div> element with className='message-container' that wraps the MessageDisplay component and both button elements.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully wrapped the content in a container div with proper styling structure.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you wrap both the MessageDisplay component AND both buttons inside a single div with className='message-container'.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's try again. You need to wrap the existing MessageDisplay component and both buttons inside a <div> element with className='message-container'.

steps.title: Export the App component
steps.instruction: Export the App component as the default export so it can be used by other modules.
steps.hint: Add the 'export default' statement before the App component declaration.
steps.expectedOutcome: The App component is exported as the default export, making it available for use in other files.
successCriteria: The code should include 'export default App' or 'export default function App'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully exported the App component as the default export. This makes it available for use in other modules.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you're exporting the App component as the default export. Check that you've added 'export default' before the App component declaration.
steps.feedbackWrong: The App component is not exported as default. Add 'export default' before the App component declaration to make it available for use.
